repo.description:
### Summary

An API key granted only `clusterGroup.read` can submit the group-wide forced people reset
(POST /api/cluster-groups/{id}/regenerate-people), although its scope excludes mutating
permissions. With facial recognition enabled, the reset deletes person metadata (names,
birth dates, thumbnail files) for face groups left without faces. Verified live on v3.3.5.

### Details

Affected: immich v3.3.5 (current release); behavior present on main as reviewed 2026-10-27.
Class: CWE-863 Incorrect Authorization - permission misclassification (the guard correctly
enforces an incorrectly assigned permission).
Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N ≈ 4.3 (Medium).

POST /api/cluster-groups/{id}/regenerate-people - "Forcefully re-run facial recognition for
all faces of users in this group" - is a destructive, group-wide operation. Its `force`
branch unassigns every ML-sourced face→person assignment in the cluster group, runs person
cleanup, runs `VACUUM ANALYZE` + `REINDEX TABLE CONCURRENTLY` on `asset_face`/`person`, and
re-queues recognition for the group's faces.

The route is annotated `@Authenticated({ permission: Permission.ClusterGroupRead })`, and
API-key authorization enforces exactly that annotation
(`isGranted({requested: [ClusterGroupRead], current: key.permissions})`,
server/src/services/auth.service.ts). So an API key granted only `clusterGroup.read` is
authorized to submit this destructive reset for the owner's entire cluster group. The
permission system itself works - the same key is correctly denied ordinary mutations - the
defect is that a mutating endpoint carries a Read permission. The project's own advisory
history treats API-key permission scoping as a security boundary (CVE-2026-23896 /
GHSA-237r-x578-h5mv, fine-grained API-key permission escape).

Prior-art note: group-wide member resets are an intentional feature (#30965) and their cost
has been publicly discussed (#32250). This report does not dispute that a full member's
session can reset their group. The boundary at issue is the credential scope: the relevant
attacker holds only the restricted key.

The same root cause has a second consequence: `Permission.ClusterGroupRead` is also granted
to pending invitees (`checkInviteAccess` in server/src/utils/access.ts), so an
invited-but-never-joined user can invoke the reset before becoming a member (dynamically
confirmed separately: 204 as invitee; outsider 400; unauthenticated 401).

## Root cause

- server/src/controllers/cluster-group.controller.ts - `regenerate-people` annotated
  `Permission.ClusterGroupRead` (a mutating endpoint carrying a Read permission).
- server/src/services/cluster-group.service.ts:75-82 - `regeneratePeople()` requires that
  Read permission, then queues `FacialRecognitionQueueAll {clusterGroupId, force: true}`.
- server/src/utils/access.ts - `ClusterGroupRead` also resolves for pending invitees
  (`checkInviteAccess`), producing the secondary consequence above.
- Contrast within the same controller: `ClusterGroupLeave`/`ClusterGroupRequestCreate` are
  member-only - the Read treatment of the reset is inconsistent with its effect.


### Proof of concept

Fresh-instance setup (official ghcr.io images, immich-server v3.3.5 + bundled postgres + redis;
steps all via the public API):
1. POST /api/auth/admin-sign-up → admin account.
2. POST /api/admin/users → regular member user (the future key owner); log in.
3. Member uploads an asset (POST /api/assets) and creates a person (POST /api/people).
4. Admin enables facial recognition: PUT /api/system-config (machineLearning.enabled: true;
   sub-setting facialRecognition.enabled is true by default). In a stock deployment with the ML
   container running, ML-sourced faces exist naturally; in our lab (no ML container) the face
   rows were inserted directly in the database - disclosed as lab setup below, and not part of
   the attack: the vulnerability is the API-key authorization step 3→4 below, which requires no
   special database state.
5. (Optional, for cluster-group variants) member creates/joins a cluster group via
   PUT /api/cluster-groups/{id}/requests + accept.

The attack itself, on the fresh instance:

1. Cluster-group member creates a read-scoped API key:

   POST /api/api-keys {"name":"readonly-integration","permissions":["clusterGroup.read"]}
   -> 201 (response body: permissions: ["clusterGroup.read"], secret)

2. The key permits member listing and rejects direct person deletion:

   GET  /api/cluster-groups/<gid>/users                     -> 200
   DELETE /api/people {"ids":["<person>"]}                  -> 403 Missing required permission

3. The same read-scoped key is authorized to submit the forced-reset request and receives
   204:

   POST /api/cluster-groups/<gid>/regenerate-people         -> 204 No Content

4. The queued force job executes and deletes the key owner's seeded ML-backed person.
   Controls: a key scoped to `asset.read` calling the same endpoint -> 403; unauthenticated
   -> 401.

Before/after (the member's own people data):

- A1 - before (API): GET /api/people -> ['Dad (seeded ML person)', 'Mom (seeded manual person)']
- A2 - before (rows): Dad: person row + 1 machine-learning face; Mom: person row + 1 manual face
- A3 - attack: POST /api/cluster-groups/<gid>/regenerate-people with the clusterGroup.read-only
  key -> 204
- A4 - after (rows): Dad's person row DELETED (name and birthDate lost; ML face unassigned).
  Mom survived - the manual face remained assigned.
- A5 - after (API): GET /api/people -> ['Mom (seeded manual person)']
- A6 - controls: same key DELETE /api/people -> 403 (scoping enforced elsewhere); asset.read key
  -> 403 on the reset; unauthenticated -> 401.

The A4 differential supports the ML-only unassignment mechanism. Deleted person metadata not
being restored by re-clustering is a source-derived conclusion (the re-cluster path creates
new records; it does not reinstate names or birth dates). Repeat calls return 204; duplicate
submissions may be deduplicated while a job remains unfinished.

Happy to share the full frozen transcript (requests with statuses, SQL before/after snapshots)
and retest a fix.


### Impact

What kind of vulnerability: broken authorization at the credential-scope boundary. A
least-privilege API key - an integration key, or a leaked/scoped-down key - held by any
cluster-group member can trigger the forced people reset, even though its scope excludes
mutating permissions.

Who is impacted: deployments using fine-grained API keys, and every member of a cluster
group. Verified live: the key owner's ML-backed person (name, birth date) was deleted by the
reset. Source analysis supports the wider reach: `unassignFaces` filters by cluster-group
membership with no caller restriction, so other members' ML-backed person groups are equally
eligible for the unassign→cleanup path - a person group loses its curated metadata when the
reset leaves it without faces (a surviving non-ML face reference preserves it; thumbnail
unlinking on deletion is source-derived).

No confidentiality impact demonstrated. The code performs server/database work (vacuum,
reindex, re-queued recognition); resource consumption was not measured, so no availability
impact is claimed. Restoring deleted names and birth dates requires manual reconstruction or
a backup.

Suggested fix: give `regenerate-people` a dedicated mutating permission (e.g. a new
`clusterGroup.reset`/`clusterGroup.update`) in both the controller annotation and the
service-level `requireAccess`, with a member-only object-access rule for it. That closes
both consequences (read-scoped keys and pending invitees) while preserving the intended
invite-preview reads (GET /cluster-groups/:id/users with a pending request is explicitly
tested behavior and should remain).
repo.summary: Read-scoped API keys can reset cluster-group people data
